q: Name the Jura's four geographic AOPs plus its two specialty appellations.
accept: arbois chateau-chalon l'etoile cotes du jura macvin cremant
arbois etoile chateau-chalon cotes du jura
ans: Arbois, Château-Chalon, L'Étoile, Côtes du Jura — plus Macvin du Jura and Crémant du Jura
exp: L'Étoile is named for star-shaped fossil crinoids in its soil.

q: What soil dominates the Jura and how does it relate to Burgundy's?
accept: marl and limestone same jurassic sequence
ans: Jurassic marl and limestone — the same sequence that surfaces across the Bresse plain in Burgundy
exp: The Jura gave the geological period its name.

q: Which Savoie crus grow Chasselas on the southern shore of Lake Geneva?
ans: Ripaille, Marin, Marignan and Crépy on the lake's southern shore
exp: The French side of Switzerland's Chasselas belt.

q: Name Corsica's three principal AOPs beyond the island-wide appellation.
accept: patrimonio ajaccio muscat du cap corse
ans: Patrimonio, Ajaccio, Muscat du Cap Corse (with Vin de Corse and its villages)
exp: Patrimonio was the island's first AOC, 1968.

q: What are 'Vin de Savoie Crus', and roughly how many exist?
accept: about 16 named crus apremont abymes chignin
ans: Around 16 named crus (Apremont, Abymes, Chignin, Chignin-Bergeron, Arbin, Jongieux…) appended to Vin de Savoie
exp: Small, alpine, and increasingly sought by sommeliers.

q: Vin de Paille du Jura: how long must the grapes dry, and what is the minimum élevage before the wine may be sold?
accept: dried six weeks then aged three years
at least six weeks drying and three years elevage
six weeks passerillage three years with eighteen months in cask
grapes dried six weeks wine aged three years eighteen months in wood
6 weeks on straw 3 years elevage 18 months in oak
minimum 6 weeks passerillage then 36 months of ageing
dried a minimum of 6 weeks aged a minimum of 3 years
ans: The grapes are dried off the vine (passerillage hors souche) for a minimum of six weeks, and the wine is aged at least three years, of which at least 18 months in wood
exp: Made from Chardonnay, Savagnin, Poulsard and Trousseau in Arbois, L'Étoile and Côtes du Jura, the bunches are laid on straw, racked or hung until they concentrate to roughly 320 g/L of sugar — so the harvest is picked early and healthy, not botrytised. Note the bottle: vin de paille goes into 375 ml, never the clavelin, which is reserved for Vin Jaune.

q: Roussette de Savoie is a single-variety appellation. Name the grape, and name two of its four crus.
accept: the grape is altesse and two crus are marestel and monterminod
altesse and the crus frangy marestel monterminod monthoux
ans: Altesse (100%) — the crus are Frangy, Marestel, Monterminod and Monthoux
exp: Do not confuse the two 'Rous-' words of Savoie: Roussette is Altesse, while Bergeron in Chignin is Roussanne. Altesse gives a firmer, more citrus-and-quince wine than Jacquère and is the one Savoie white with real cellar life; Marestel, on steep limestone above Lake Bourget, is the benchmark cru. Altesse also supplies Seyssel.

q: Savagnin Blanc is genetically identical to which variety, and how does Gewurztraminer relate to it?
accept: it is traminer and gewurztraminer is a mutation of it
same grape as traminer gewurz is the pink aromatic mutant
traminer with gewurztraminer as a berry colour mutation
savagnin is traminer gewurztraminer is a clonal mutation
savagnin blanc is traminer and gewurztraminer is savagnin rose aromatique
the same variety as traminer with gewurztraminer as its aromatic pink skinned sport
ans: Traminer — Savagnin Blanc and Traminer are one variety under two names; Gewurztraminer is its pink-berried aromatic mutation (Savagnin Rose Aromatique)
exp: One ancient variety, three faces: Savagnin Blanc in the Jura, Traminer in Austria and the Alto Adige, Gewurztraminer as the aromatic pink-skinned sport. Savagnin is also one of the most genetically important grapes in Europe — a confirmed parent of Silvaner and Grüner Veltliner, and an ancestor of a wide family across eastern France and the south-west. Knowing the link explains the wine: ouillé Savagnin's high acid and citrus-pith bite is Traminer's, not something the voile created.

q: Savennières' two grand-cru-like sub-appellations are Coulée de Serrant and:
exp: Coulée de Serrant is Nicolas Joly's biodynamic monopole — 'the Montrachet of the Loire' (Curnonsky).

q: Quarts de Chaume gained which unique Loire distinction in 2011?
ans: The Loire's only Grand Cru AOP (botrytized Chenin)
exp: Minimum 298 g/L must weight; Bonnezeaux and Coteaux du Layon surround it.

q: Which Sancerre commune's terres blanches sites — Les Monts Damnés and Le Cul de Beaujeu — are home to the Cotat and Vatan cult bottlings?
ans: Chavignol (Monts Damnés, Cul de Beaujeu on Kimmeridgian marl; the silex soils lie east, around Sancerre town and Ménétréol)
exp: Also home of Crottin de Chavignol — the canonical pairing.

q: The three soil types of Sancerre are silex, caillottes and:
exp: Caillottes: shallow limestone gravels for early-drinking charm; terres blanches for structure; silex for smoke.

q: Which appellation makes only sparkling wine around Saumur by tradition, with tuffeau cellars, and hosts Bouvet-Ladubay and Ackerman?
ans: Saumur Mousseux (Crémant de Loire production also centres on Saumur)
exp: Ackerman brought the traditional method to the Loire in 1811.

q: Match the appellation to its grape.
exp: Romorantin survives only in Cour-Cheverny; François I planted it.

q: Beyond the base AOP, Muscadet Sèvre-et-Maine and Muscadet Coteaux de la Loire are joined by which other subzone?
exp: Sèvre-et-Maine bottles ~80%; the crus communaux (Clisson, Gorges, Le Pallet…) add long-lees tiers.

q: What is the minimum lees-aging for Muscadet crus communaux like Clisson?
exp: The crus demand extended sur lie (17–24+ months) and taste like it: saline, tensile, age-worthy.
